Questions 19 to 26
You are going to read a story about Irfan Lim, a robotic genius. For questions 19-26, choose
the correct answer (A, B, C, or D) and mark the correct letter A, B, C, or D on your answer
sheet.
Irfan Lim was a fourteen-year-old robotics genius who lived in Cyberjaya, Malaysia's technology
hub. He attended the prestigious Malaysia Institute of Technology despite his young age, thanks
to his exceptional talent for creating robots. His older brother, Hakim, was a final-year student at
the same university and often encouraged Irfan's inventions. Hakim was everything Iifan wanted
to be - brilliant, popular, and confident. The brothers had lived with their Aunt Faridah since their
parents passed away years earlier.
One night, Hakim took Irfan to the university's robotics lab to show him something special.
There, Hakim revealed his latest creation - a healthcare robot called Bayu. Unlike other robots,
which can be defensive, Bayu was designed with a friendly, non-threatening appearance, like a
large white balloon with simple black eyes. Hakim had programmed Bayu with thousands of
medical procedures and given him a caring personality. The robot could scan anyone and
provide immediate healthcare assistance.
Tragedy struck that same night when a mysterious fire broke out in the laboratory building.
Hakim rushed back inside to save his research and never returned. The authorities ruled it an
accident, but Irfan was devastated by the loss of his brother.
Weeks after the funeral, Irfan discovered Bayu in his room, apparently brought home by Hakim
before the fire. When Irfan accidentally activated the robot, Bayu immediately scanned him and
diagnosed his emotional distress. The healthcare robot began looking after Irfan, attempting to
help him recover from his grief.
While testing Bayu's capabilities, Irfan discovered a microchip in his brother's lab coat. The chip
contained information about strange experiments and referenced a company called Mega
Technology Industries. When Irfan inserted the chip into his computer, it revealed a hidden
laboratory where Hakim's research was being used without permission.
Committed to investigating his brother's work, Irfan decided to upgrade Bayu with defensive
capabilities to protect them. He was joined by his university friends: Zara, a chemistry expert;
Rizal, a mechanical engineering student; Danish, a speed-loving transportation specialist; and
Lily, who specialised in electromagnetic technology. Together, they formed a team to uncover
the truth about Hakim's research.
The team discovered that Professor Ahmad, a respected technology leader, was secretly using
Hakim's research to build dangerous microbots. These tiny robots could form any shape and
cause massive destruction when controlled by a neural transmitter. Professor Ahmad had
started the laboratory fire to steal Hakim's work and eliminate any competition.

ING/1/5
Irfan and his friends created special suits with unique abilities to enhance their skills. Zara could
create chemical reactions, Rizal had super strength with his mechanical arms, Danish moved at
incredible speeds, and Lily generated electromagnetic fields. Irfan developed a suit that allowed
him to communicate with and program Bayu for different situations.
When Professor Ahmad unleashed his microbots on the Putrajaya government district, Irfan and
his team rushed to stop him. During the confrontation, they learned that Professor Ahmad
blamed the technology industry for personal tragedies in his past. Bayu scanned Professor
Ahmad and identified his emotional trauma, which helped Irfan understand the man's pain.
In the final battle, Irfan realised that defeating Professor Ahmad wouldn't heal anyone's pain.
Instead, he used Bayu's healthcare programming to offer help for the professor's emotional
wounds. Though the professor initially rejected their assistance, Bayu's gentle persistence
eventually broke through his anger.
After Professor Ahmad was taken into custody, Irfan understood that his brother's true legacy
wasn't just robotics innovation but the desire to help others. He decided to continue developing
Bayu's healthcare abilities while using technology to protect Cyberjaya with his friends. The
team became known as the Cyber Heroes, with Bayu serving as both a healthcare provider and
guardian for the city, fulfilling Hakim's dream of using technology to care for people.

Part 4
Questions 27 to 32 are based on an article about shopping as therapy for health.
Six sentences have been removed from the article. Choose from the sentences A to H the
one which fits each gap (27 to 32). There are two extra sentences which you do not need to
use.
Mark your answers on the separate answer sheet.
SHOPPING AS THERAPY FOR HEALTH
Shopping may prolong life, at least for the over-65s in Taiwan, according to recent
research.27.
Men and women who shopped daily lived longer than those who refrained
from retail therapy, say scientists who examined thousands of people over several years.
According to a report published in the Journal of Epidemiology & Community Health,
shopping may provide companionship, exercise and an opportunity to maintain a healthy diet
28.
Researchers believe shopping offers a range of social and physical benefits that can
improve health outcomes.
In the study, Dr. Yu-Hung Chang and his team examined the lifestyles of nearly 2,000
men and women aged 65 and over who lived independently. 29.
Even after adjusting for
variables such as age, gender, and existing medical conditions, the link between shopping
frequency and survival remained strong.
Interestingly, they found that regular shoppers were more likely to have better mobility
and cognitive function compared to those who rarely shopped. 30.
This may be because
shopping entails walking, decision-making and interpersonal interaction—all important activities
for maintaining health.
Some researchers argue that shopping may help create a routine and instil a sense of
purpose. Engaging in simple activities like browsing and choosing items can give people control
over their daily lives, which is essential for mental well-being. 31.
David Oliver, a visiting professor of medicine for older people at City University, London,
supported the findings. 32.
The activities such as walking through shops and socialising
while shopping benefit older adults significantly.
However, experts also advise moderation. Although shopping can promote better health,
it should not lead to reckless financial behaviour. Excessive shopping or spending beyond one's
means can cause financial stress and negatively impact health.

Here are six people sharing their views on giving freedoms while managing expectations. Read
the texts below and answer the questions that follow.
Giving Freedoms While Managing Expectations
A - Maria, 16
I think teenagers need freedom to grow. My parents let me choose my hobbies, and that helps
me feel trusted. But they still expect good grades and respect. It's not always easy, but |
understand their rules. Freedom with clear expectations helps me become more responsible.
Without rules, I might not take life seriously.
B - Janne, 15
In my opinion, too much control is bad. I want freedom to make my own choices. At the same
time, 1 know my parents want the best for me. They expect me to study hard and be polite. I
think it's fair if freedom comes with trust. If I break that trust, I understand I'l lose some
freedom.
C -Aisyah, 17
Freedom is important for learning. When I make mistakes, I learn from them. My parents let me
go out with friends, but they expect me to come home on time. I think that's a good balance. !
feel more confident and grown-up when they give me space but still guide me with clear rules.
D - Leo, 19
Sometimes, I feel like adults don't understand how much freedom we want. I know they worry
about us, but being too strict can push teens away. I believe we need space to make small
mistakes. If parents explain their expectations kindly, it's easier to follow them. Freedom and
respect should go both ways.
E - Emma, 16
I believe freedom with limits is the best way to grow. If I only did what | wanted, I might forget
what's important. My parents let me choose my own clothes and friends, but they expect me to
be honest and kind. I like that they trust me. It makes me want to do better.
F - Daniel, 18
I think teenagers should have some freedom to choose their path. For example, I enjoy art
nore than science, and my parents support that. But they also expect me to do my best in all
subjects. It's not always fun, but I understand their point. Freedom is great, but without goals
it's easy to waste time.
